findings.finding: The spec highlights that the `bootstrapper` test suite (which includes the parity drift guard, the `SAFE_ARG` contract, and the quoted command handling) currently does not run in CI at all, and no CI jobs run on Windows. This makes the security-load-bearing drift guard purely dependent on local developer discipline to run tests before committing.
findings.suggestion: Add a lightweight step to your CI pipeline (ideally on a `windows-latest` runner, or at minimum `ubuntu-latest` for the drift-guard assertions) specifically targeting the `bootstrapper/test/` suite. This correctly surfaces the falsification tests on future PRs.

findings.finding: For `openBrowserPlan` (`cmd.exe /d /s /c start "" <url>`), Probe 32 correctly verifies that the outer quoting handles command metacharacters like `&` in the URL. However, if the underlying URL string ever unexpectedly contained a raw double-quote character (`"`), it would terminate the `cmd.exe` quote block prematurely, potentially allowing trailing input to be evaluated as a command.
findings.suggestion: Apply a `.replace(/"/g, '%22')` to the URL payload immediately before constructing the verbatim `/c start "" "<url>"` string. This removes the only character that can break out of a verbatim double-quoted argument in Windows CMD.  Overall Assessment: This is an exceptionally rigorous and practically engineered approach to a notoriously tricky Windows vulnerability. The decisions to rely on tested verbatim duplication over cross-package dependencies, and to deliberately decouple binary resolution from version validation, strictly adhere to boundary constraints without over-producing.  SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: approve

findings.finding: The resolver’s injected `platform` and its path implementation can disagree. The plan explicitly acknowledges that Windows branches use the host `path` module, meaning Linux CI exercises POSIX path parsing even when `platform === "win32"`. This is particularly risky for PATH splitting, drive-letter paths, backslashes, absolute/path-like detection, and spaced-path quoting—the exact security-sensitive behavior being changed. Existing local Windows probes establish one machine’s behavior, but the automated tests will not reliably catch regressions.
findings.suggestion: Make path semantics follow the effective platform: use `path.win32` whenever the resolver is evaluating a Windows plan (and `path.posix`/host path as appropriate otherwise), or inject a `pathImpl` alongside `platform` in tests. Add assertions using actual Windows-style paths while running on Linux so CI validates the same branch deterministically.

findings.finding: The documented behavior for unresolved bare commands is internally inconsistent. The Spec Impact section says `defaultRun` returns `ok: false` “without spawning” for an unresolvable tool, but the Store-alias remediation deliberately falls back to spawning the unresolved bare command so `CreateProcess` can invoke App-Execution-Aliases. A genuinely absent tool will necessarily take that same fallback and emit an `ENOENT`/error event before producing `ok: false`.
findings.suggestion: Correct the stated contract and tests to distinguish “not resolved by explicit PATH/PATHEXT scanning” from “not spawned.” The actual contract should be that unresolved bare names may receive one shell-free `CreateProcess` attempt, and all failure modes still return the existing non-throwing `ok: false` verdict. If no-spawn absence is truly required, define a reliable alias-specific detection mechanism—which is unlikely to be worth the added complexity.

findings.finding: defaultOpenBrowser` still sends a URL through `cmd.exe /c start`, and quote-wrapping alone does not establish safe handling for all `cmd.exe` expansion modes. In particular, `%VAR%` expansion occurs inside double quotes; caret and delayed-expansion behavior also has subtle context-dependent rules. The cited browser test covers `&`, but the plan does not clearly establish that percent expansion, exclamation marks, quotes, CR/LF, and caret combinations are either safely encoded or rejected. Since URLs can commonly contain percent-encoded data, simply rejecting `%` would also be a meaningful compatibility decision.
findings.suggestion: Define one tested URL-to-`cmd.exe` encoding contract rather than relying on generic argument quoting. Prefer a Windows-native opener invocation that avoids interpolating the URL into a command line if practical. If `start` remains required, explicitly reject control characters and implement/test CMD-specific escaping for `%`, `!`, `^`, `&`, `|`, `<`, `>`, and quotes, with real Windows execution fixtures for representative combinations. Do not infer CMD safety from `windowsVerbatimArguments`; that only controls Node’s argument serialization, not CMD parsing.

findings.finding: The remediation has no continuing Windows execution gate. The source scan prevents reintroducing `shell: true`, but cannot validate PATHEXT resolution, `.cmd` execution, `cmd.exe` quoting, App-Execution-Alias fallback, or browser-plan startup. The assertion that this is “requires-physical-device” is not compelling for these process fixtures: a `windows-latest` CI runner can execute purpose-built `.cmd` files and exercise the relevant branches. In addition, the bootstrapper suite currently does not run in CI at all.
findings.suggestion: Add a focused Windows CI job for this change, at minimum running the bootstrapper tests and a real `.cmd` fixture in an unspaced directory, a spaced directory, and an `&`-containing directory. It need not validate opening a real browser; that path can test process creation against a controlled command/fixture or retain the existing local evidence. This turns the one-time developer-machine verification into durable regression protection.

findings.finding: Importing `resolveSpawn()` from `preview-win32-spawn.ts` introduces a new ESM cycle on the server boot path. The plan notes it is safe today because neither module currently performs module-load work, but that is a fragile invariant rather than a robust module boundary. This change makes version probing dependent on preview-session module initialization order, and a future top-level export/value change can produce partially initialized bindings or startup-only failures unrelated to the caller.
findings.suggestion: Either break the dependency cycle before merging by placing the resolver in a dependency-neutral module, or add an explicit boot/import-order regression test and document the cycle at both import edges. Given this is security-sensitive spawn plumbing and `cli-compat` runs during boot, avoiding the cycle is preferable if the ADR guard permits a pure relocation of the shared helper.

findings.finding: Exporting `SAFE_ARG` and `openBrowserPlan` as new published-package API solely for testability unnecessarily expands the support surface of a package with no `exports` map. These helpers encode security-sensitive implementation details and could become de facto public contracts once consumers import them.
findings.suggestion: Keep the new resolver module importable for tests if needed, but avoid exporting helpers that callers do not need. Test the plan through the module’s intended resolver/opening entry point, or use package-internal test imports. If these exports must remain, document them as intentionally supported API and add compatibility expectations accordingly.  Overall, reusing the reviewed resolver and retaining a small, tested package-local mirror is sound, and the plan has unusually strong local Windows evidence. However, the platform-path mismatch, unresolved-command contract contradiction, CMD URL escaping requirements, and lack of a durable Windows execution gate should be addressed before considering the change complete. SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise

On POSIX, `resolveSpawn()` is intentionally a pass-through, so an absent `claude` proceeds to `spawnSync("claude", ...)`. `spawnSync` returns an `ENOENT` error with empty stderr, and this function returns that empty stderr rather than the required `"claude not found on PATH"` verdict. The explicit not-found behavior is only implemented for the Windows resolver-null branch.
findings.suggestion: Translate `r.error?.code === "ENOENT"` into the same `{ ok: false, code: null, stdout: "", stderr: "claude not found on PATH" }` result after `spawnSync`, and add a POSIX absent-command assertion.

findings.finding: The `.cmd` wrapper only quotes tokens containing whitespace and interpolates all other tokens directly into the command string passed to `cmd.exe`. CMD metacharacters such as `&`, `|`, `%`, `!`, `^`, `<`, and `>` in a no-space target or argument are therefore parsed by `cmd.exe`, not passed literally. This affects the newly exported generic `resolveSpawn()` and `defaultRun(cmd, args)`, whose arguments are not charset-gated; it also makes valid paths such as `C:\tools&more\tool.cmd` fail or potentially execute an unintended command.
findings.suggestion: Implement CMD-safe escaping/quoting for every token in the command line, including percent/delayed-expansion handling, or reject CMD metacharacters at this generic boundary and keep callers constrained to safe arguments. Add Windows execution tests for metacharacters in both a resolved `.cmd` path and an argument.

findings.finding: spawn()` reports executable-launch failures asynchronously via its `"error"` event; the surrounding `try/catch` does not catch them. Because the returned child has no error listener, a bad `ComSpec` value or unavailable opener can emit an unhandled error and terminate the bootstrapper, contradicting the “Never fatal” contract.
findings.suggestion: Store the child returned by `spawn`, attach a no-op/error-handling `"error"` listener before calling `unref()`, then unref it. Preserve the existing nonfatal behavior by logging or ignoring that error as appropriate.

findings.finding: The new probe-spawn suite exercises only `probeClaudeVersion()` (the synchronous probe). It does not invoke `probeClaudeVersionAsync()` under the Windows `.cmd` and spaced-path branches, despite the specification explicitly requiring both probes to be remediated. A regression restoring `shell: true`, omitting `windowsVerbatimArguments`, or using the wrong plan in only the async probe would pass this suite.
findings.suggestion: Add async tests using a mocked `spawn` child process that records command/options and emits stdout plus `close`; cover direct `.exe`, `.cmd`, spaced `.cmd`, and spawn-error behavior.  Overall assessment: The core shell-removal approach is sound and most acceptance criteria are implemented, but the POSIX not-found contract and unsafe CMD token construction need correction before shipping. SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise
